query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Direct aging of the as-built, supersaturated fcc alloy to form L1₂ and L2₁ precipitates will stabilize the microstructure by creating diffusion barriers that slow oxygen ingress and intergranular oxidation, thereby mitigating the rapid degradation and catastrophic failure observed during high‐temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with a supersaturated fcc matrix lacking significant precipitate structure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled direct aging heat treatment designed to promote the formation of coherent L1₂ and partially ordered L2₁ precipitates.
generation.conditions: Expose both as-built and aged samples to isothermal elevated temperatures (e.g., ~800–1000°C) under controlled oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of L1₂ and L2₁ precipitates that act as barriers to fast grain-boundary and lattice diffusion paths, thereby hindering the rapid transport of oxygen and reactive species along susceptible paths.
generation.mechanism: By forming precipitates, the aging treatment reduces the effective diffusivity of oxygen and delays the development of interconnected oxide scales and intergranular embrittlement. This limits the evolution of microcracks and the progression to catastrophic failure under high-temperature service environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built state, the aged samples will exhibit slower oxide-scale growth, reduced intergranular oxidation, and delayed initiation and propagation of cracks; thus, they should maintain superior mechanical integrity over an extended exposure time.
generation.baseline: The as-built, non-aged alloy exposed under identical high-temperature oxidizing or reducing conditions.
generation.boundary: The effects are expected to manifest within the high-temperature range (approximately 800–1000°C) and under both oxidizing and reducing gas exposures, where traditional fast diffusion contributes to degradation.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the optimal aging parameters (temperature and time) to consistently form the desired precipitate phases, as well as the potential differential behavior under reducing versus oxidizing environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples: one left in the as-built state and one subjected to a heat treatment to induce L1₂ and L2₁ precipitate formation. Expose both sample sets to an isothermal environment at around 900°C under carefully controlled oxidizing and reducing atmospheres. Regularly monitor changes in microstructure, oxide layer thickness, and crack initiation and propagation over time.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology via SEM/EDS
Precipitate structure and distribution via XRD and TEM
Intergranular oxidation extent using high-resolution microscopy
Mechanical integrity (e.g., fracture toughness or crack growth resistance) via standardized mechanical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation kinetics (oxide growth and intergranular oxidation) and an improvement in resistance to crack initiation/propagation compared to the as-built samples, or if the formation of L1₂ and L2₁ precipitates does not correlate with the observed improvements.
